_comment: Animal realm naming reference. Personal names and place names generated from inside each birth's worldview (perspectivism). Place names reflect what the creature notices, values, and remembers — not geography as outsiders see it. Personal names reflect what parents hope for children, or what the community observed at birth. Use these pools when writing event NPC names, companion names, and location flavor text.

ocean._comment: The ocean as the naga, karka, matsya, and makara experience it — ancient, territorial, layered by depth and current. Nothing here is accidental. Every feature has been claimed or contested.

landscape_features._comment: Shared ocean geography. These names appear in any ocean zone event text.

naga.naming_philosophy: Naga hold lineage as the deepest form of identity — a name is an inheritance, a claim, a record. Children are named for what the parent hopes they will carry into the future: a current, a memory, a way of holding still. Naga names are fluid, vowel-heavy, sinuous in the mouth. A naga who has held the same thermal current for a century may rename themselves after it. Place names are events remembered: not where something is, but what happened there and who was present.
parent_wishes: May you carry the old water

karka.naming_philosophy: Karka value endurance above all things — what is built, what is held, what does not crack. Names are given late, after the child's shell has begun to harden into its characteristic pattern. A name given too early is considered bad luck: you have named a thing before it has proven itself. Karka parents say: 'May nothing crack you.' Place names are functional and precise — defined by thermal output, structural integrity, depth to bedrock.
parent_wishes: May what you hold outlast you

matsya.naming_philosophy: Matsya are the most present-tense of all births — they live in the immediate movement of the shoal, in the collective turn. Individual names are given by the shoal, not the parents, and usually describe the child's behavior in their first week. A matsya who always turns left at the decision point becomes Leftward. A matsya who sees the shadow first becomes Shadowwatch. Names are short because they need to carry fast across water.
parent_wishes: May the shoal know your turn
May you be fast without hesitation
May the light find you in deep water
May you always be in the middle

makara.naming_philosophy: Makara are so ancient and solitary that their naming traditions are barely traditions — more like geological habits. They rarely name children; often a young makara goes unnamed until they have held a territory for a season, at which point they name themselves after its most characteristic feature. Place names are simple, definitive, and never change. 'The Trench' has been the Trench for longer than anything else in the ocean has a name.

forest._comment: The forest as eight overlapping territories — no creature sees the whole of it. Every tree is a claim, every stream a boundary. The forest is not a place; it is an aggregate of contested presences.

rakshasa.naming_philosophy: Rakshasa are intensely solitary and dislike compound identities. A name should be one clean word, like a strike. Parents name children late — not at birth but at the first successful hunt, which is when a rakshasa becomes someone worth naming. Before that, they are simply 'the young one.' Place names are possessives: not 'The Ridge' but 'My Ridge.' Not 'The Territory' but 'My Territory.' They use personal place names rarely, only when speaking to others.
parent_wishes: May you be the one who is not found
May you be solitary and sufficient
May you need no one and want for nothing

varaha.naming_philosophy: Varaha are deeply communal — the sounder is the unit of identity, not the individual. Names are given at birth and reflect the circumstances: the quality of the earth beneath the birth-site, what the sounder was doing, what the weather was doing. A child born during heavy rain near good tubers might become Mudblessed. A child born when the sounder was moving fast through danger becomes Runborn. Names are warm, round, earthy.

shardula.naming_philosophy: Shardula are solitary and precise. They pay close attention to light — the quality of dappled forest light is the aesthetic foundation of their world, both for hunting and for beauty. Names often refer to moments of perception: the instant before action, the quality of stillness, the particular light of a given hour. A parent says: 'May you see and not be seen.' Place names describe functional qualities of terrain: cover quality, sight-line distance, how the light falls at different hours.

May the spotted light find you

gana.naming_philosophy: Gana name children for resonance: what the pack will hear of them. A name is meant to carry across a valley and come back changed by the distance, so the good ones are built out of sound before they are built out of meaning. A gana who has not yet been heard at range is not considered fully named.

May your howl carry the valley
May the song live in you
May the hunt find you worthy

mriga.naming_philosophy: Mriga name children for alertness: what they will notice that others miss. The name is a claim about attention, and it is tested early — a fawn is called by it from out of sight, and how fast the head comes up settles whether it fits. Like the gana they hold that a name should carry across a valley, but for the opposite reason: theirs has to be heard by someone already running.
parent_wishes: May you hear what others miss
May the alarm sound through you
May the trail hold your memory
May you be first to know and last to be found

vanara.naming_philosophy: Vanara naming is semi-serious — they understand names matter but cannot resist making the moment funny. A child named at birth gets a formal aspirational name. A child who does something memorable in their first year often acquires a second name that sticks better. The formal name is used in ceremony; the second name is used in everything else. Parents say: 'May you laugh last,' which sounds like a blessing but is also practical advice.

May you be too quick for consequence
May the fruit be there when you arrive

yaksha.naming_philosophy: Yaksha are guardians by nature — they define themselves by what they hold, not what they pursue. Names are formal, often compound, and describe a function as much as a person. A yaksha child is named at the moment they first demonstrate awareness of a boundary — when they stand at the edge of something and know, without being told, that they must not let it be crossed. Place names are ancient, maintained across generations, and often coincide with actual boundary markers.

May you be remembered at the contract
May your word bind as well as stone

dura.naming_philosophy: Dura measure everything in depth and duration. A name should describe what endures — what goes below, what is made carefully, what roots support. Children are named at the moment they first help dig: they take a stone from the tunnel, they carry earth up and out, and in that moment the sounder watches to see how they work. The name comes from the quality of that first effort. A deliberate child becomes Careful-Layer. A strong child becomes Deep-Strike.
parent_wishes: May what you make outlast you
May you know what is below

khadga.naming_philosophy: Khadga are in no hurry — they name children slowly, watching first. A newborn khadga may go unnamed for an entire season while the parent observes. When the name comes, it is final and heavy, like a footfall. Khadga do not give children aspirational names; they name what they see. A calm child: Stillness. A heavy child: The Great Weight. A child who charges the wall of their enclosure repeatedly: Perhaps the Wall Matters.

bhramara.naming_philosophy: Bhramara individual names are ceremonial constructions given by the hive mind collectively. What the hive names you is what you are. Names describe roles compressed into sounds — a long title reduced to something that can be waggle-danced in seconds. The individual barely matters; the function matters entirely. Place names are extremely precise: defined by flower species, altitude, humidity, and time of day.
parent_wishes: May the flower know your name
May you find the right flower
May the hive never lose you

patanga.naming_philosophy: Patanga naming is aspirational to the point of ecstasy. They name children for what the child will burn toward. A name is a trajectory. To name a child 'Flame-Seeker' is not prediction; it is summoning. Patanga names are given at the moment of first strong light-response — when the infant turns instinctively toward any source of brightness. That first turn is the name.
parent_wishes: May the light find you worthy
May you choose the fire that illuminates

sky_distributed._comment: Sky births live across all three zones but share a vertical orientation — they measure the world in altitude, thermal quality, and wind. Their place names are mostly aerial; their ground-level place names are functional minimums.

shyena.naming_philosophy: Shyena measure the world in height and angle. Their territory is not the ground below but the airspace above it — measured in altitude bands, thermal columns, and sight lines. A name should describe either a quality of speed or a quality of vision. Children are named at first flight: what the parent saw in the first stoop tells them the name.

kapota.naming_philosophy: Kapota name things by the history of information that passed through them. A tree is named for the most important message ever relayed from it. A waypoint is named for the journey that established it. Personal names commemorate arrivals and departures — the moment of return is considered most naming-worthy. 'The One Who Came Back' is always an honored name. In the Conference of the Birds, every pilgrim is renamed upon arrival.
parent_wishes: May you know all the routes
May the flock gather at your call
May you be the one who comes back

uluka.naming_philosophy: Uluka are the most deliberate namers of all births. They watch a child for a full season before naming. What is observed in that season becomes the name — not what is hoped, but what is seen. 'You cannot name what you haven't watched,' they say. Place names are named for specific events of perception: what was heard there, what was seen from there, what was understood in that location for the first time.
parent_wishes: May you see what others miss
May you understand before you act
